title: idea · don't manage context — tag content so it's queryable
body: Julian (11:4x): we don't need to MANAGE context, we need to TAG content so it's queryable — a fresh agent should be able to query for asides, ideas, whatever. Implication: tags become a first-class dimension on events (this very event carries a tags array as the first instance — extra fields pass the intake since the registry only checks required). Wants: tag vocabulary worth settling lazily; query surface (fold by tag); probably an aside/idea event kind eventually instead of overloading thread. Replaces handoff-style context management with retrieval — same direction as the no-handoffs ruling.

text:
Both flagged in the log, and the second one got exercised in the act of recording the first: both events carry a `tags` array (`aside · idea · design · later` and `idea · design · context · agent-interface`) — the intake passes extra fields, so tags work *today* without any schema change. That's the first real instance of the pattern: the tag vocabulary can settle lazily, by use, the same way everything else here has.

`T-inkswitch-topos` — the marriage, flagged open, with the note that it's already structural rather than aspirational: the drag-and-drop olog you just reacted to is literally Ink&Switch's tactile-software tradition holding a Topos olog. The two houses already met in that frame; the aside is about making the marriage intentional.

`T-tagging-not-managing` — the principle itself, as its own record, with the implication chain: tags as a first-class event dimension (proven by these very events), a fold-by-tag query surface, probably a proper `aside`/`idea` kind eventually instead of overloading `thread`, and the framing that this *replaces* context management with retrieval — which is the no-handoffs ruling taken to its conclusion.

And noted: the holy shit was for the drag-and-drop olog view. That's the design signal — the strongest reaction of the session came from touching the category theory, not reading about it. Worth remembering when deciding what to build next.

Yes — and the best part is that this isn't a new idea bolted on; it's the generalization of something the lexicons already do. Look at `paper.node.json` and `paper.box.json`: each already has a `render: { element, template, ephemeral }` section. That *is* the trait, embryonically — a per-kind declared presentation. Your move names it and promotes it:

**The trait reading, mapped onto our machinery:**

- **`tilable`** = "I declare a default presentation for tiled contexts." Concretely: a lexicon's `render` section. The tiler never knows what a node *is* — it queries the trait. No subtyping: nothing inherits from "tile"; a kind just *declares* it, exactly like `derives`. The graph stays kind-agnostic at the store level; presentation knowledge lives entirely in the vocabulary layer (lexicons), which keeps the three-machines cut clean — render is a projection that dispatches on declared capabilities, not on types.
- **`interactable` / `widget`** = tilable *plus acts*: the lexicon's `acts` section (guard, event, via) plus registered gestures. A doc box is tilable but not interactable; a box node is both; the distinction is which sections the lexicon declares. Traits compose by section, not by hierarchy — `tilable ⊂ interactable` is "interactable lexicons also carry a render section," not inheritance.
- **The frame** stops being a hardcoded builder and becomes *a tiling of node references* — a frame is a layout whose slots are filled by nodes (or a query selecting nodes), each presenting via its own trait. Our `FRAMES` array and `frame_def` markdown are then just two degenerate cases: a static frame is a fixed tile-list, and a `frame_def` is a tilable node whose presentation is markdown.

And the **olog designer** is the first real instance of the full chain: it's a node of a kind that declares both traits — presented as the playground with its edge layer, interacting via the link/move/resize gestures whose acts are `node`/`edge`/`box_geometry`. The thing you dragged this morning stops being "frame 5" and becomes *the olog designer widget, tiled into a frame* — instanced anywhere, twice if you want two views of the same graph.

Two design questions this opens, both worth settling before building:

### ▸ B · Where does a node's trait-ness live — type, instance, or both?

The Rust analog is precise: `derives` is per-*type*, not per-value. So the candidate is: traits live in the lexicon (all nodes of kind `olog-designer` present the same way), while instance-level payload carries only *parameters* — which olog it shows, seed layout, geometry. But there's a real case for node-level override (a specific node wanting a custom presentation), and that's the "projector writes md that humans also edit" tension from the bootstrap handoff resurfacing one layer up. My candidate: type-level only, overrides deferred until a use demands them — same laziness as everything else.

### ▸ C · Is a frame itself a node?

If frames are tilings-of-nodes, the natural completion is that a frame is *also* a node in the graph — an object whose payload is the tile-list/query. That unifies frame switching with the graph (frame layout becomes persisted, shareable, projectable), and `frame_switch` events become navigation within one structure. It also means the olog designer can eventually show *frames as nodes* — the system sketching itself at one level higher. Cost: it entangles presentation state with domain nodes right where we've been keeping them apart, so the frame-node's payload has to be honest about being presentation-layer data.

If you rule on those, the smallest first build under this design is clear: **promote the sketch frame into the `olog-designer` widget node** — write its lexicon with explicit `tilable`/`interactable` declarations (render + acts sections, already half-written), tile it into a frame by reference instead of a hardcoded builder, and leave the general tiler to grow around the one real instance. One widget, trait-declared, is worth more than a tiling system designed from imagination.

title: design · schemas are arrow profiles; traits couple orthogonal domains
body: Julian (11:52): revisit schemas from the categorical/type lens. What we write are declarative types where data are behavioral properties. A node is not a thing-with-data; it is a thing with arrows in and out, some of which are identity arrows to literals (attributes). A trait is a coupling between ORTHOGONAL types — tileability does not depend on any data that makes a node its kind; different semantic/conceptual domains, which is why traits work where subtyping fails. Agent sharpening: the three machines (domain/system/render) are exactly the orthogonal domains; a lexicon section is a declared trait-coupling; a lexicon is a conjunction of couplings for one kind. Attribute-as-arrow means nodes have no intrinsic data — two nodes with identical arrow profiles are indistinguishable; fold-id (object identity) is separate from arrow profile, which is why relabels keep identity. Schema file = presentation of a small category sketch (fields = arrows to literals, edges = arrows to objects, required = arrows that must exist) plus couplings.

text:
Logged as `T-schemas-as-arrow-profiles` (tagged `design · category-theory · types · schema` — the tagging principle paying for itself two flags after being minted). Now the sharpening, because I think your framing has one more consequence hiding in it:

**The three machines were the orthogonal domains all along.** Look at what a lexicon file actually contains: `domain` (fold/states/acts), `system` (tick/ingest), `render` (element/template/ephemeral). Those sections *are* the trait couplings — `paper.box`'s render section couples box-ness to the presentation machine, its acts section couples it to the domain machine, its system section to the engine. The lexicon isn't a type definition with data; it's a **conjunction of couplings between orthogonal conceptual domains**, one per machine. Subtyping fails precisely because it would have to flatten those domains into one hierarchy — "a widget IS-A tilable IS-A node" pretends presentation knowledge lives below kind knowledge, when actually they never touch. The sections keep them parallel, and a kind can couple to any subset.

**Attribute-as-arrow makes "no intrinsic data" literal.** If every field is an arrow to a literal object — and the literal's only arrow is identity, which I take to be your point: literals have no structure to traverse, so the arrow terminates — then a node has *nothing inside it*. What we've been calling "the node's data" is just its outgoing arrows to literal-objects plus its arrows to other nodes. Two consequences worth having:

- **Indiscernibility falls out for free**: two nodes with identical arrow profiles are the same node, period. Which is the formal version of something we already do — the fold key (`id`) is *object identity*, deliberately separate from the arrow profile, which is why a node can relabel itself (change its label-arrow) and remain the same object. The id isn't data; it's the name of the object the arrows are about.
- **Validation becomes arrow-checking**: "required fields present" reads as "the declared arrows must exist." A schema file is then a presentation of a small sketch: fields are arrows to literals, edges are arrows between objects, and eventually composition laws are declared paths. Nothing new needs to be built for this reading — the registry already behaves this way — but it tells us what the schema files *are* when we do revise them: not record layouts, arrow vocabularies.

And the Rust analogy lands exactly where you put it: `derives` compiles to a dictionary of capability-impls dispatched independently of the type hierarchy — our render dispatch is a functor from the domain olog into the presentation olog, *defined only on the objects that carry the coupling*, and undefined (not inherited, not defaulted) elsewhere. A node kind without a render section doesn't present badly; it doesn't present.

The open edge of this I'd flag rather than resolve: **edge lexicons carry composition**, and composition is the one place the arrow-reading demands something we haven't written — when is a path through intermediate objects *itself* an arrow of the graph? That's the category question from `paper.edge.json`'s UNDESIGNED note, and your framing says the answer will be a declared law, not an inference. First use that earns it is probably the olog designer letting you ask "what's connected to what, transitively" — and then we write it.

Logged, then. Where the design thread leaves the build queue, when you want to pick it back up: promote the olog sketch into the `olog-designer` widget node (first trait-declared instance — ▸ B and ▸ C still open on where trait-ness lives and whether frames are nodes), and behind it, the schema revision as arrow-vocabularies rather than record layouts.

Nothing needs deciding right now — the plane's there when you want your hands back on it.

Here's the list, grounded in what ologs actually demand (Spivak's well-formedness rules are mostly *readability* rules — that shapes what "check" means below). Ordered by when each gets earned, tactile first:

**Authoring — getting an olog onto the plane**

1. **Create a node by hand.** Double-click empty plane → inline name field → commit = `node` act. (Today only I seed; you can't add one without me.)
2. **Rename in place.** Double-click a label pill → inline edit → relabel act, same id, identity preserved (the arrow-profile point: the label-arrow changes, the object doesn't).
3. **Retype in place.** Cycle/pick `node_kind` (object, machine, functor, view…) — probably a small affordance on the pill or a radial, not a form.
4. **Inline verb-phrase write-in on drop.** The rubber band lands, a small inline field appears on the arrow — type, enter commits. This retires `prompt()`, which is currently the weakest thing in the widget.
5. **Edit an existing arrow.** Grab its *midpoint label* (same gesture grammar: by-name grab = relate) → re-verb, or re-drop the endpoint on a different node = redirect. Same edge id, folded.
6. **Supersede, not delete.** A dismiss gesture (flick off-plane? select + ⌫) = supersede act; fold drops it from view, history keeps it. Ologs get redrawn constantly — erasure must be cheap but never destructive.
7. **Pan and zoom.** The floor olog already strains one screen; the canvas wants to be unbounded. Also the natural precursor to multi-olog layouts.
8. **Box-select and bulk move** — earned when rearranging stops being node-by-node.

**Reading — what makes it an olog and not a diagram**

9. **Path-to-sentence.** Select a chain of arrows → the widget composes them into prose: "the event log folds into the graph, which is quotiented by a claim." This is the signature olog move and it's *also* the composition check (below) wearing its presentation clothes.
10. **Views/quotients as first-class.** Declare a subgraph ("show me only the machines," "only the floor olog") — a view is a node of type view whose payload is a selection; the widget renders it as a filtered plane. This is where the claims-quotient machinery gets its tactile twin.

**Checking — the new territory**

11. **Inline well-formedness marks, linter not gatekeeper.** Checks present as badges on the offending node/arrow, never block editing:
    - dangling arrow (endpoint node missing/superseded)
    - ambiguous arrow — two arrows, same source, same verb → the "is" reading breaks; olog arrows are functional by discipline
    - bare arrow (legal, flagged — some arrows are just structure)
    - typing complaints, kept loose: a functor-typed node with no arrows in/out; a machine claiming to relate to a literal
12. **Reading-as-the-type-checker.** A path that *reads grammatically* is admissible composition; a path that stumbles ("the log, which is wanted by a ruling via a card…") is either a genuinely new insight or a badly-verb'd arrow. The check is you reading the composed sentence — the widget's job is to make the sentence and mark where it creaks.
13. **Every complaint cites its evidence.** Click a mark → the events that produced the offending structure (the history functor as *error provenance*). No unexplained red.

**Behavioral requirements of the system** (these constrain how the above is built, and a couple want rulings):

- **Checks are pure folds, never stored.** A check result is derived presentation, recomputed per render — no check events, no dual-write seam. This follows ruling 6 but is worth stating because lint state is exactly the kind of thing that tempts storage.
- **Presentation never invents domain facts** — so a *mark* is ephemeral; a *dismiss/supersede* is an act. The line between them is the line between seeing and ruling.
- **Everything is one log.** I author with the same acts you do (already true — I seeded the floor olog by hand this morning); conflicts resolve by fold, latest-per-id, on both sides.
- **The widget itself is trait-declared** — every feature above lands as lexicon sections (acts for gestures, render for presentation), so the olog designer is the reference instance of `interactable`.

Two genuine open rulings hiding in the list: **supersede semantics** (what does the fold do to an edge whose endpoint was superseded — dangle-and-mark, or cascade?) and **whether a view-declaration is an act or a presentation preference** (I lean act — a quotient is a domain fact about how you read the graph, not a window preference). Flag those when you're ready; the build order I'd propose is 4 → 1 → 6 → 9 — inline write-in, hand creation, supersede, then path-to-sentence, which is where checking is born.

title: design · nondeterministic checks: teeny agent calls through the act intake
body: Julian (12:0x): the olog widget also TESTS how to do nondeterministic checks for real-time feedback with teeny-tiny agents/llm calls — e.g. how do we verify noun-phrase rules? Agent candidate: verdicts are acts by actor:linter, through the same lexicon-validated intake as gestures (check event kind, schema-checked output, rejected if malformed); two-speed checking (deterministic folds render synchronously, LLM marks arrive async and styled softer); batch one call per settled graph state (debounced, no-edit quiescence), cache by content hash so unchanged labels are never re-asked; nondeterminism is deterministic AT REST — the call may vary, the recorded verdict does not; verdicts are candidates not rulings, every mark cites its verdict event (history), dismissal is a ruling act that pins an override. Open: verdicts-as-events vs ephemeral cache (agent leans events); call granularity per-label vs per-graph.

text:
Logged (`T-nondeterministic-checks`). And the design answer, I think, is hiding in something we built this morning without meaning to:

**The linter is just another author.** A noun-phrase verdict is an act — `{kind: "check", actor: "linter", target: "n-fold", rule: "noun-phrase", verdict: "ok" | "smell", proposal: "a fold"}` — posted through the same `/act` intake as your gestures. That single move answers most of the hard parts at once:

- **The nondeterminism is deterministic at rest.** The *call* may vary run to run; the *recorded verdict* doesn't. Once it's an event, it's foldable, auditable, and queryable by a fresh agent — which the ephemeral-cache alternative never is. The mark on your screen renders by folding check events, exactly like everything else.
- **The same validation floor catches model slop.** The LLM's output must satisfy a `paper.check` lexicon or the drain rejects it — malformed hallucination dies at the intake, the same place a malformed gesture dies. Schema discipline turns out to apply to model calls for free.
- **Every complaint already cites its evidence.** Click a soft mark → the check event → the label event it judged. History-as-provenance was already the pattern.

**The real-time feel comes from four cheap disciplines, not from the model:**

1. **Two speeds.** Deterministic checks (dangling, ambiguity, typing) are pure folds — synchronous, instant, styled as hard facts. LLM marks arrive whenever they arrive and render visually *softer* (dashed, grayed) — you should never wait on one or mistake one for a fact.
2. **Batch per settled graph, not per keystroke.** One teeny call per quiescent state: the whole visible graph as compact JSON, one prompt — "for each node label: is it readable as 'a/an X'? if not, propose the form" — returning a list of verdicts. One round trip checks everything on screen.
3. **Cache by content hash.** A label that hasn't changed is never re-asked; the fold sees the latest verdict per (target, rule) and a relabel simply generates a new ask. Token cost is bounded by your *editing*, not your viewing.
4. **Ask for the fix, not just the flag.** The verdict carries a proposed noun-phrase ("the graph (folded)" → "a graph, folded from the log"). The proposal *is* the evidence — you read it and either take it (an act) or dismiss it (a ruling act that pins an override, so the linter learns your dialect and never nags that one again).

The honest open question — and I flagged it in the log rather than deciding it: verdicts-as-events means the log grows with every check, and a chatty linter could bloat it (mitigation: batched verdicts as *one* event per settle, superseded by the next). The alternative — ephemeral cache — keeps the log clean but makes checks invisible to every future session, which cuts against the retrieval-over-management ruling from an hour ago. I lean events; the cost is the thing to watch once it's real.

And your meta-point stands: this widget is the testbed for a pattern much bigger than ologs — *any* system where tiny model calls provide standing feedback needs exactly this shape: validated intake, recorded verdicts, softer-than-facts presentation, adjudicable dismissal. If it works here it works for prose checks in the reader, schema checks in the lexicons, claim-confidence scoring in the quotient views. Worth building slowly and honestly, because it's a reusable organ.

title: design · logs are unions/queries, not one thing
body: Julian (12:1x): doubts the single giant log as the right abstraction. Logs themselves are unions/queries — if everything is a derived view, views can derive over as many things as necessary, not just one. Agent resonance (rejected-atproto still donates shape): atproto is exactly this — per-DID repos as base logs, the firehose a derived union view with its own merged sequence. Consequences: base log = one serialized writer (order stays local and total per log); the union needs a merge order (ts now; the CRDT/automerge change-unit question when writers go concurrent — that is the earned future, not now); ids qualified per log; actor routes acts to their home log. This structurally dissolves the check-bloat worry (linter verdicts live in their own log; views select whether to union them). First real user: the linter — checks.jsonl as the second log. Design-by-use move: generalize the fold input from one log to a SET of declared log slices (unit 3 already said declared inputs); physical sharding follows need, the query surface leads. Floor restated: the floor is not the log, it is the LOGS (many append-only streams); the single events.jsonl was a degenerate union of one.

text:
Logged (`T-logs-as-unions`). And I think you're right, with one sharp observation to add: **we've seen this shape before, in the thing we rejected.** atproto is exactly this architecture — per-DID repos are the base logs (each a total order from one writer), and the firehose is a *derived union view* with its own merged sequence number. We ruled out adopting it, but its skeleton answers your question almost clause by clause: base logs per serialized writer, unions as queries, cursors that work over the merge.

The pivot restated cleanly: **the floor isn't the log, it's the logs.** `events.jsonl` was a degenerate union of one — which was correct when there was one writer and one fold, and is exactly why it held together this long. What the union view buys:

- **Order becomes local.** The thing the single log actually provided was a total order via one serialized drain. That's still true *per log* — each base log is one writer's total order (you, me, the linter, boot). The union's interleaving is derived, and until writers go concurrent, timestamp-merge is honest; when they do, the merge order question *is* the automerge change-unit unit we've had queued all along. The union view doesn't create that problem — it names where the problem lives.
- **The check-bloat question dissolves structurally** instead of by mitigation. The linter's verdicts live in `checks.jsonl`; whether the main view unions them in is a *query decision*, not a data-format decision. Same for any future chatty standing program.
- **Folds already wanted this.** Unit 3's standing programs were specced as "pure functions of a log slice, declared inputs" — the plural was there from birth. `foldGeometry` over the geometry log, the olog fold over a union of node/edge logs + geometry log, the context card over everything. Declared inputs means a fold *cites its sources*, which is the queryability principle applied to computation itself.
- **Views compose.** A quotient view (claims) over a union of logs is just a fold whose input is another fold's output — and if logs are queries, then the whole system is one kind of thing: queries over queries, with append-only streams at the leaves.

The design-by-use move, so this doesn't become a big-bang restructure: **don't shard the file yet — generalize the query surface first.** The fold API takes "a set of declared log slices" instead of one log; the physical world can stay one file until a second log *earns* existence. And the first candidate is already standing in the queue: the linter. `checks.jsonl` as the second log, unioned into the widget's view, is where multi-log gets its first real user — small, reversible, and it carries both of this session's threads (nondeterministic checks and logs-as-unions) in one build.

One honest cost to name: the single log made "no dual-write seams" trivially true — one append, one fold surface. N logs means an act needs a *home* (my candidate: actor routes — your acts to your log, linter verdicts to checks, mine to mine), and ids want qualifying (`log:id`) once collisions are possible across streams. Both are small, but they're the coordination the single log was quietly doing for free, and they should be decided by ruling, not by drift — the yjs report's exact warning, one layer down.

title: ruling-candidate · each node gets its own log
body: Julian (12:03): the home is simpler than actor-routing — EACH NODE GETS ITS OWN LOG. That is what he was reaching for with logs-as-unions. Consequences (agent sharpening): (1) history(n) was already this — the fold⊣history adjoint becomes literal: a node history IS a union query over log(n) plus the logs of nodes pointing at it (edges are nodes, so an edge act homes in the edge-node's own log; incidence is derived by join — no fan-out dual-write). (2) no id collisions (ids local per log), order local per log, the drain routes by node id. (3) everything-is-a-node means even messages/frames/checks are nodes with logs — the old events.jsonl is the union view / firehose over all node logs, derived and rebuildable. (4) tactile user feature earned: open a node, see its log — click into any box and read its history inline (the history functor as a navigation gesture). Physical shape: nodes/<id>.jsonl; union as materialized derived index; global cursor = firehose seq. Open: is there any primitive global stream at all, or only per-node logs + unions?

text:
Logged (`T-node-logs`). And yes — this is the clean version, and it retroactively explains why the adjunction felt right: **`history` was already a per-node log.** The history functor's action — "take this node back to the events it came from" — *is* the query "union the logs of this node and everything incident to it." You weren't reaching for something new; you were naming what the right adjoint had been all along.

The picture once it lands:

- **A node's log is its home.** Acts route by node id; order is local and total per node (one writer's stream per thing); ids never collide because they're only ever local. The drain's validation story survives untouched — it just gains a routing key.
- **Edges don't break it, because edges are nodes** — that ruling from this morning pays off immediately. An edge act's home is the edge's *own* log; it doesn't need to write into two endpoints' logs (no fan-out dual-write). "Incident events" is derived: `history(n) = log(n) ∪ { log(e) : e ↦ n or n ↦ e }` — a union query, a join through edge-nodes. Everything you said about unions does the work here too.
- **The old `events.jsonl` demotes to a firehose** — the union view over all node logs, derived and rebuildable, exactly the atproto shape. It stays useful (that's what polls and cursors read) but it stops being the *authority*; the node logs are.
- **Everything is a node, so everything gets a log** — messages, frames, checks, cards. The linter's verdict homes in the *checked node's* log (or the check-node's), and "is the log bloated" stops being a question: no node's log is bloated unless one thing is genuinely being edited to death, which is... its history, correctly so.

And it earns a tactile feature for the olog designer for free, which is how you know it's the right abstraction: **open a node, see its log.** Click into any box and its history unfolds inline — every geometry change, every relabel, every check verdict, *with the union view showing what's incident to it*. That's the history functor as a navigation gesture, and it's the debugging and trust surface for the whole system: nothing is unexplained because every node carries its own explanation.

The one open edge I flagged in the log rather than papering over: **is there any primitive global stream left at all?** Some things felt streamy rather than nodey — chat flowing in, frame switches, session heartbeats. My candidate: those are all nodes too (a message is a node; a session is a node; its log is the stream), so no — nothing primitive survives except per-node logs and unions. But that's a ruling-sized claim, because it decides whether the drain needs a "global" fallback home for acts that name no node, and I'd want your ruling on it before the shape is load-bearing. The first build stays what it was: the linter as the second log, except now it's not `checks.jsonl` — it's verdicts homed in the checked nodes' logs, and the union reading them in.

title: ruling · the floor is the type — divorced from instantiation, divorced from time
body: Julian (12:0x): THE FLOOR IS THE TYPE — the thing divorced from instantiation and from time. The stack: lexicons (types, timeless, edited out-of-band in git, never events) → node logs (temporal, per node) → folds/unions (derived views). Each node log is a functor from its local time-order into the floor category; folds are colimits of those diagrams; history is the diagram itself. Validation gains its meaning: the intake checks that every temporal act instantiates a timeless type — instantiation is the one-directional bridge (types constrain acts; acts never mutate types; type changes stay out-of-band). Confirms this morning's candidate (the floor olog is the event grammar) and supersedes T-node-logs' open question: nothing primitive is temporal except node logs; types are the primitive beneath even those.

text:
Logged as a ruling (`T-floor-is-the-type`, closed). And it clicks the whole morning's stack into place — three levels, each divorced from the next by exactly one thing:

- **Types (the floor): timeless.** Lexicons, the vocabulary, the arrows-that-could-be. No ts, no actor, no instantiation — which is why they live as files edited out-of-band in git and hot-reload into the registry, and why that arrangement stops being an implementation accident and becomes *the principle*: type changes are not events, and nothing in the log can mutate a type. Time never gets into the floor.
- **Node logs: time.** Each node's log is — and this is the formulation your sentence was reaching for — a **functor from its local time-order into the floor category**. An event isn't a thing with a timestamp; it's an instantiation of a timeless type, *positioned* in one node's timeline. That's all the temporal layer is: diagrams drawn in the floor.
- **Folds: derived.** And then folds stop being an implementation trick and become **colimits of those diagrams** — hydration is the colimit of a node's geometry diagram ("what position survives the whole history"), the olog view is a colimit over node and edge logs, the union firehose is a bigger diagram. And `history` is nothing but *the diagram itself* — which is why fold ⊣ history felt structural all session: colimit and diagram, the universal property and the thing it summarizes.

What this ruling settles, concretely:

1. **Validation now has a theorem-shaped meaning.** The drain's check — "required fields present" — is the assertion that a temporal act instantiates a timeless type. Instantiation is the *only* bridge between the layers, and it's one-directional: types constrain acts, acts never touch types. Every schema-checked thing in the system (gestures, seeds, and — per the linter thread — LLM verdict calls) crosses the same one-way bridge.
2. **The open question from T-node-logs closes: no primitive global stream.** Nothing temporal is primitive except node logs; beneath them is the type layer, and beneath *that* is nothing. `events.jsonl` is fully demoted to a derived union.
3. **Design effort has an address.** You said it this morning before it was a ruling — the lexicons are where intent concentrates. Now it's load-bearing: the floor is the only layer a human designs directly; everything above it accretes by use.

One caution to leave at the edge, not as an objection: "divorced from time" is a *discipline*, not a fact — the schema files do change, in git, by our hands, on a Tuesday. The ruling keeps that change out-of-band on purpose. The cost is that the log can never explain why the floor changed — no history functor reaches the type layer. If that ever itches (and git blame may not scratch hard enough), the temptation will be to make type-edits events. The ruling says: don't — that would put time inside the floor and collapse the stack. Better to keep a *projection* someday (types → a read-only view in the log) that preserves the divorce while making it visible.

title: ruling · the floor is the type — outside time; instances live in runtimes
body: Amended per Julian (12:1x): the distinction is types vs INSTANCES. Types are outside of time — though their definitions obviously change over (meta-)time, i.e. git, out-of-band. An instance of a type NECESSARILY lives in some runtime. Instantiation = placement: an instance is the pattern plus a WHERE — which runtime, which node log, which position in it. Our stack has one runtime so far (the paper), so runtime was invisible — degenerate case again. Consequence: runtime becomes a dimension; same type instantiated in two runtimes = two instances until sync merges them (the yjs/automerge future gets its home here). Seam to watch: folds read old events against CURRENT type definitions; a log is a diagram indexed by time into a category that itself moves in meta-time — atproto NSID versioning exists for exactly this.

text:
Right — I collapsed two things that your sentence keeps apart: the type is outside *time*, but its definition moves in *meta-time* (git, our hands, Tuesdays), and an instance isn't a type-occurrence, it's a type **placed in a runtime**. Instantiation is the *where*, not just the *what*: which runtime, which node's log, which position in it. That's a cleaner floor than mine, and it exposes a dimension that's been invisible all session because it's degenerate:

**We have exactly one runtime.** The paper's server-and-page is the only place instances exist, so "runtime" never had to be a coordinate. But the moment it becomes one — and the node-log ruling plus the sync future (yjs state vectors, automerge change units) both point there — it's the *third key* on every instance: type, time, runtime. The same type instantiated in your browser and in a fresh agent's context are two instances, two timelines, until a sync merges them; and merge is then a functor question, not a file-format one.

One seam your formulation names better than mine did: **folds read old events against current type definitions.** A node's log is a diagram indexed by time, drawn in a category that itself moves in meta-time — strictly, each old event instantiated the type *as it was then*. Today the registry validates at intake-time and the fold trusts it forever after, which is fine while lexicons only *add* fields. The moment a definition breaks an old event's shape, that's where versioning gets earned — and it's worth noting atproto's NSID versioning (`paper.node.v1` → `v2`) exists for precisely this, which is the second time today a rejected adoption has donated a shape back.

title: design · monoids: the algebra under the whole stack
body: Julian (12:2x, one word): monoids. The unfolding: a node IS a one-object category — its own history is its endomorphism monoid (events as the node acting on itself: created→moved→renamed). A node log = the FREE monoid on its type's generators (word = the log, length = time). A fold = monoid homomorphism from the free monoid to a state monoid (S, merge, unit) — the lexicon's domain.fold section DECLARES the target monoid; LWW-per-key is Map with keyed merge; hydration = foldl; the poll live-half = incremental homomorphism application. Sync across runtimes = merging words of free monoids; concurrent independent events commuting = TRACE monoid (Mazurkiewicz) — the precise algebra of the automerge change-unit question. Home-rolled CRDT design = choosing the state monoid (associative, commutative, idempotent merge = convergence). The graph = many monoids (nodes) plus arrows between them (edges).

text:
Yes — and it's the right one word, because it's the algebra that every layer of this morning turns out to have been doing unawares:

- **A node is a one-object category.** Its own history — created → moved → renamed → linked — is its *endomorphism monoid*: the events are the node acting on itself over time. That's the precise version of "a node isn't a thing with data, it's arrows" from an hour ago: the incoming/outgoing edges are the arrows to *other* objects; the log is the monoid of arrows to *itself*. The graph is many monoids plus arrows between them. That *is* a category, now genuinely, not metaphorically.
- **A node's log is the free monoid** on its type's generators. The log is a *word*; time is word length; append is the monoid operation; the empty log is the unit. Nothing temporal is anything but a word over the type alphabet.
- **A fold is a monoid homomorphism** — from the free monoid (word) to a state monoid `(S, ⊥, ·)`. This is what the lexicon's `domain.fold` section has been all along without saying so: it *declares the target monoid*. Last-write-wins is `Map` with keyed merge; hydration is `foldl`; the poll's live-half re-fold is the homomorphism applied *incrementally* — which is why "fold on every render" was always affordable: homomorphisms don't need re-reading the word, they need the new letter.
- **And the sync future gets its exact name:** merging words from two runtimes, where independent events commute and conflicting ones don't, is a **trace monoid** — Mazurkiewicz traces, free *partially*-commutative monoids. That's the algebra hiding inside "automerge change-units" and the union-merge question from the logs-as-unions thread. The home-rolled CRDT ruling, restated in one line: *CRDT design is choosing the state monoid* — pick `·` associative, commutative, and idempotent, and convergence across runtimes is a theorem instead of an aspiration.

The payoff of naming it: monoid homomorphisms compose, so folds compose (quotient views over union views over node logs — queries over queries, now with a legality proof); and every future "how do two things merge" question has a checklist — what's the alphabet, what's the state monoid, is the map a homomorphism — instead of a design argument.

One honest limit, so the lens doesn't overclaim: the *type* layer isn't monoidal — it's the presentation (alphabet + laws) that the monoids are free on. Types are what the monoid view *presupposes*. Which is consistent with the ruling you just made: the floor stays outside all of this algebra, because the algebra is what happens in time.

title: design · one architecture, N ticks: presentation is ologs too
body: Julian (12:3x): if each instance is monoidal, each object IS its own log and its current state is the fold; and if UI presentation is also ologs, it is the SAME ARCHITECTURE but the tick is for rendering (a la a UI lib). Agent unfolding: the three-machines ruling collapses into one mechanism instantiated at different ticks — domain machine folds on the drain/event tick, presentation machine folds on the rAF/pointer tick, engine on the poll tick; the lexicon system section declares WHICH tick. Consequences for the olog widget: (1) the widget is itself a node with its own log; state = fold; ephemera are unlogged letters by ruling (R3 lineage), not a different kind of state. (2) folds become incremental homomorphism application — a new letter updates only its node state, render reprojects the touched thing; no more full refold scans. (3) presentation objects (tile, pill, edge-layer, rubber band, drawer) are objects typed by presentation lexicons with arrows among themselves; render is a functor presentation-olog → domain-olog-reading, the adjunction already ruled. (4) open ruling: which presentation letters are logged — frame/view selection is domain-ish (frames-are-state ruling), viewport pan/zoom/scroll likely ephemeral (vault lineage).

text:
Logged (`T-one-architecture-n-ticks`). And the answer is: it changes the widget *less* than you'd fear and *more* than you'd expect — because the three-machines ruling, restated in this framing, is that **the three machines were never three kinds of thing; they're one mechanism instantiated at three ticks.** Domain folds on the drain/event tick, presentation folds on the rAF/pointer tick, engine on the poll tick. The lexicon's `system` section — "when it ticks and where it reads" — was already the declaration of *which tick*. Everything else is shared machinery.

Concretely, what changes in the olog widget:

**1. The widget is itself a node with a log; its state is the fold.** The olog designer stops being a hardcoded frame and becomes an instance of type `olog-designer` whose log records its letters: which view is active, what's selected, pan/zoom. Ephemera (the rubber band, the in-flight drag, the half-typed verb phrase) aren't a *different kind of state* — they're unlogged letters, exactly the R3 lineage ("gestures, not records") now with algebraic standing: a gesture is a word you haven't committed to the monoid yet. Commit = release = the letter enters the log; the fold absorbs it; the projection updates.

**2. Folds go incremental — this is the real implementation win.** Today `foldGeometry` rescans `latest` on every render; the poll live-half refolds everything. Under the homomorphism view that's wasteful and wrong-shaped: a new `box_geometry` letter updates exactly one node's state (keyed merge, one Map entry), and the render *reprojects only the touched thing*. A UI library's whole trick — dirty components, not full re-render — falls out as "apply the letter, reproject the delta." The widget gets a UI-lib render loop *without a UI lib*, because monoid homomorphisms were always incremental and we just weren't exploiting it.

**3. Presentation objects are olog objects.** Tile, node-pill, edge-layer, drawer, rubber band — each is an object typed by a *presentation lexicon* (with its own render/acts sections), arrows among them (`tile presents a node`, `edge-layer connects two pills`). Render is then literally a functor from the presentation olog *into a reading of* the domain olog — which is the act/render adjunction you ruled this morning, finally with both sides typed. The nice property this buys: **the presentation layer can be sketched in the olog designer itself** — the system drawing its own UI as nodes and arrows, one level up from the floor olog sketch. The widget's own presentation olog is data we can inspect, check, and redesign on the plane.

**4. The ruling this forces (and I'd flag rather than decide):** which presentation letters get logged? Frame/view selection is already ruled domain-ish ("frames are state"). Pan/zoom/scroll — my candidate is *ephemeral*, vault lineage (scroll position was always projection, never record): viewport is how you look, not what you mean. But selection is genuinely on the fence — selection-as-pointing feels like the record-bracket speech act (you're showing me something), selection-as-editing-prelude feels ephemeral. When you select two nodes and draw between them, the whole gesture is one letter anyway; when you select and *stare*, that's a demonstration and wants logging.

So the build under this framing: the widget's own log + incremental keyed-merge folds + a `render()` that reprojects deltas instead of rebuilding — which is also, note, the exact shape the general tiler needs when frames become tiles of trait-declared nodes. The olog designer stops being a special frame and becomes the first full citizen of the architecture it designs.

title: ruling · logged vs ephemeral is decided per-instance, by need
body: Julian (12:14): the logged/ephemeral question is answerable by NEED — do you actually need to detect change over time of a datum? If not, ephemeral. And this can vary PER INSTANTIATION: a version of olog-designer where you want certain letters logged where this use case doesn't. So: the TYPE declares the alphabet (which letters can exist); the INSTANCE carries a logging policy selecting which are emitted — unit 3's policies slot, now with a home. The need-test in our vocabulary: does any fold need the history functor defined on this datum — is there an adjunction that wants its right adjoint here? Asymmetry to remember: promoting a letter to logged gains history only from that moment forward; the un-logged past is gone (.paper-offset lesson). Policies grow by use; start minimal.

text:
Logged as a ruling (`T-logged-by-need`). And it slots into the machinery almost suspiciously well, because unit 3 specced standing programs as "pure functions of a log slice **+ policies**" — the policies slot existed with nothing in it. Now it has a first meaning:

**The type declares the alphabet; the instance carries the policy.** `olog-designer`'s lexicon says which letters *can* exist (view_select, pan, zoom, selection, gesture_commit…); each instance's payload says which are *emitted* — a per-instantiation logging policy. That's the same move as the trait ruling, one layer over: variation between instances is *data*, never a subtype. There's no "AuditOlogDesigner" type; there's an olog-designer with a different policy.

And your need-test has an exact translation into this morning's vocabulary: **do you need the history functor defined on this datum?** Logging a letter is precisely what makes `history` exist for it — makes it a word in the monoid that a right adjoint can walk back. If no fold anywhere needs to distinguish its past states, there's no adjunction asking for its right adjoint, and ephemeral is correct, not lazy. That's also a clean retroactive reading of R3: drawer state and in-gesture geometry have no fold that reads their history, so they were never letters — we just didn't have the test yet.

One asymmetry to keep in view, because it's the only teeth the test has: **promotion only buys the future.** Flipping a letter from ephemeral to logged starts history *at that moment*; the unrecorded past doesn't come back. That's the `.paper-offset` lesson in general form — deciding "we don't need this" is a bet, and losing it costs exactly the interval between the bet and the discovery. Which argues for the policy starting *slightly* generous around anything a future session might want to ask a fresh agent about (the retrieval-over-management principle again), and strictly minimal around the genuinely private — viewport, scroll, hover.

So the widget's first policy, under the ruling: log `view_select` and gesture commits (already events); leave pan/zoom/hover ephemeral; selection logs *only when it terminates in an act* (drawing, dismissing) — selection-and-stare stays free until a use shows up wanting to detect demonstrations. And policies are per-instance data, so the next olog designer — the one auditing how a design evolved — just turns more letters on.

title: ruling · logged vs ephemeral: do you need it differentiable along this dimension?
body: Addendum (12:1x), math-speak version: a letter is logged iff you need the datum DIFFERENTIABLE along that dimension — i.e. the map t ↦ datum(t) must exist as a path you can take finite differences of. Ephemeral = point-sampled only. Gloss: fold = integration (state = ∫ letters, monoid accumulation), history = differentiation (walk back down to letters); fold ⊣ history is ∫ ⊣ d. Policy = choosing which observables are smooth (have paths) vs point-sampled, per instance.

text:
Exactly — and that gloss upgrades the adjunction from structural metaphor to calculus: **fold is integration, history is differentiation.** State = ∫ letters — the monoid accumulation of the stream; `history(n)` = walking back down to the letters that produced it. `fold ⊣ history` is ∫ ⊣ d: the universal property of the colimit is the discrete fundamental theorem of calculus, and the widget's incremental rendering is just "integrate the new letter only."

So the need-test in math speak: **a letter is logged iff you need the datum to be a path** — iff `t ↦ datum(t)` must exist with finite differences you'll actually take. Ephemeral means you only ever point-sample the value: no path, no derivative, nothing to detect. And the per-instance policy is then choosing *which observables of this instance are smooth* — pan/zoom stay point-sampled (you never ask "how did my viewport evolve," you ask "where is it"), view selection goes smooth because its trajectory is the thing you're asking about (how did the design session move through frames).

The one place the analogy earns its keep beyond elegance: differentiability is exactly what a *fresh agent* needs. A query like "show me the asides" or "how did this claim's confidence move" is a request for a path — a section over time — and it's unanswerable against point-sampled data. The retrieval-over-management principle turns out to be a smoothness requirement: **log what you might someday need gradients of.** Point-sample what you'll only ever read at a point. That's the whole policy calculus, and it's per-instance because which gradients matter is a fact about the *use*, not the type.

text:

Two things worth noting about how it was dispatched, because they're firsts:

title: bug pattern · coding subagents returning empty output, no side effects
body: Second instance (2374a17d, olog widget build, 16:17-16:25): coding subagent ran ~8min, returned empty output, made zero changes to repo (verified: no commits, no files, working tree diff was all main-session activity). First instance: 58f2b906 (collision review, last night). Pattern is real, not anecdotal. Workaround: verify side effects before trusting status=done; re-dispatch. Watch: is it role/model-specific?

text:

Read both. Here's what composition means in each, and they point the same direction.

From the paper (Spivak & Kent, §4, read via pdftotext of the PDF on your shelf): ologs do **not** compose by merging into one big olog. An "information system" is a *diagram* of ologs — each a separate world-view with its own language (underlying graph) — connected by **functors**: alignment links that map each type to a type and each aspect to an aspect-or-path, i.e. translating dictionaries between languages. The shared understanding is the **colimit** of that diagram: a core language where the component specifications flow together, get unioned, and interact through *entailment*; results flow back to each part. The machinery is an adjunction: direct flow ⊣ inverse flow. Crucially, the parts stay heterogeneous and independent — the alignment links are the "common ground," and communication happens *through* them, not by flattening everyone into one canvas. Functors also do data migration: once aligned, instance data transforms coherently between world-views.

From your vault, the same idea appears twice in your own vocabulary:

- **ctree design threads** (threads.yaml): "level-invariant SVO style with per-level verb census; leaves as near-atomic attributed triples (olog-compatible)" with "END(i)≈START(i+1) chain checking" — composition as *type-matched chaining*: a chain is admissible exactly when the object of one triple is the subject of the next. That's your path-to-sentence, and its "chain check" is exactly our dangling/composition checks. The vault convention "a dated journal entry links an undated standing note" is the same shape: two layers, composed by explicit links, never flattened.
- The vault itself is the Kent picture lived: journal (events) and topic folders (state) as separate languages, `threads.yaml` as the alignment/intent graph over them, canvas files as projections — a community of heterogeneous documents connected through declared links.

So the amendment to my sheets candidate (thread D): **sheets, yes — but sheets alone are the wrong half.** Isolation isn't composition; the missing piece is the **alignment layer**. Concretely, in our event-sourced grammar that means:

1. `sheet` on nodes/edges keeps languages separate (a path-to-sentence reading never crosses sheets by accident — matching the paper's "same graph = same language" homogeneity).
2. A new act kind — `paper.align` — declares a functor between sheets: node→node, edge→path. The registry can *validate* it (endpoints of mapped edges must map to endpoints — functoriality as a lint, which is the T-nondeterministic-checks ruling getting its first job).
3. A composed view: fold the alignment diagram and render the colimit — both sheets in one plane with cross-sheet alignments drawn as their own stroke style, readable as a translated sentence: *"fold"* (floor) `≅` *"foldNodes"* (code) — the functor literally translates the reading.

That gives the editor its actual product shape: an olog is a document; documents stay sovereign; composition is a declared, checkable, first-class act — never a merge. The floor-olog ↔ code-olog pair becomes the first aligned diagram, which is also the mental-model audit you wanted: the alignment functor is the argument that my transcription matches your head, and you adjudicate it arrow by arrow.

Right — I was reaching for the mechanism again. Let me actually do the thing: think the project through in olog, as a design language, before any of it is code.

First, an honest observation about where we stand: the floor olog is *not* an olog yet, in Spivak's discipline. It has types and aspects, but no **facts** — no commutative diagrams, no path congruences. Spivak's definition is a category: objects, arrows, *and a congruence relation on paths*. Two-thirds of the language is missing from our editor, and facts are where the reasoning power lives: a fact says "this path equals that path," which is exactly a claim about the world that can be true or false. Our path-to-sentence composes readings but can't *equate* two readings. If ologs are the design language, facts are the first real gap — not because the tool lacks a feature, but because the design conversation can't be had without them.

With that discipline in mind, here's a first cut at the project's own ontology — types as noun phrases, aspects as functional arrows (each target unique per source — this constraint is the discipline, it forces decisions), written as claims, not code:

> **a log** —has as letters→ **an event**; —is appended to by→ **an act**
> **an event** —has→ **a timestamp**, —has→ **an actor**, —has→ **a kind**
> **a kind** —is validated by→ **a lexicon** — which —lives in→ **the floor** (git, timeless)
> **an act** —is an→ **event** that —passed→ **validation**
> **a fold** —takes→ **a log** —returns→ **a state** ; a fold —is declared by→ **a lexicon** (the domain.fold section)
> **a state** —projects onto→ **a view** ; **a view** —is seen by→ **an eye** (pan/zoom — no log fact)
> **a node** —has as identity→ **an id** ; —has as presence→ **a label** ; presence —is retracted by→ **a supersede**
> **a document** (sheet) —has as language→ **a graph** — which —has→ **types and aspects**
> **an alignment** —maps→ **a type of one document** —to→ **a type or path of another**

Already the discipline bites, in useful places — the facts we *can't yet state* are the open foundational questions:

1. **Is a supersede an event or a fact about events?** We ruled "latest per id wins" — that's a fold, i.e. a function. But is "X supersedes Y" an aspect of events (Y *is superseded by* X) or a letter in its own right? In the olog, these have different shapes, and our implementation chose one without the theory being written.
2. **What is identity?** A node *has as identity* an id — fine. But a **frame**, a **sheet**, a **lexicon** — do they have ids in the same sense, or different identity principles? (Your thread C: "is a frame itself a node?" — that's this question.) The vault answers it one way for notes (folder+HHMM), git another way for files (content hash), the log a third (id field). Three identity principles in one project, unstated.
3. **Is time an aspect or an axis?** Events *have* timestamps; but lexicons live in meta-time (git history) and views in no time at all. An olog forces this into the open: either time is a type in the olog with aspects, or it's the ambient category the whole olog sits in. Right now it's both, silently.
4. **What does an alignment preserve?** If alignments are functors, they must preserve declared structure — but we haven't declared the structure (see: no facts). You can't say what a functor preserves until the theory says what there *is* to preserve. So the composition question is *downstream* of the facts question.

That's the order I'd argue for: **facts before composition** — the congruence layer is both the missing third of the design language and the precondition for saying anything precise about how ologs compose. The thinking order isn't "add a facts feature," it's: write the project's olog, including the facts we believe, and watch which ones we can't write — each unstatable fact is a foundation not yet poured.

Does this cut match what you meant by foundations — or is the move you want even more radical: the olog *replaces* the design conversation (rulings, threads, prose specs) as the medium, rather than accompanying it?

Agreed — and it's the honest version of "ologs as design language": a theory you *run*, not a diagram you stare at. S-expressions are already the right notation for this (`(fact (= (has owner) (is owned by)))` reads as what it is — a path equation), and checks become computations instead of opinions: functoriality of an alignment is a program, congruence closure is a program, "does this olog have orphan types" is a program. Design-by-program also dissolves your (c) complaint at the root: the model stops being *reflected* in the code and starts being the code.

One thing worth noticing before we pick a substrate: **we already have a live lisp in the runtime** — `lisp.ts` + `stdlib.scm`, with `eval` acts flowing through the validated queue (`boot.scm` is literally a program that folds the log and manifests a frame). So there are two honest forks:

**Racket (or similar) as a workbench.** Contract system, pattern matching, a REPL built for thinking — an olog library comes together in hours, and foundations get explored at full speed. The cost: it lives *outside* the runtime. Designs wouldn't flow through the log; they'd be research notes to reimplement — which is a pattern we've already ruled (ruling 2: research reports = specs to reimplement). Right tool for the *thinking* phase.

**The hosted scheme as the home.** Build `olog.scm` into the runtime's own lisp, and design-by-program happens inside the event-sourced world: constructing an olog is a program, checking it is an `eval` act, verdicts land in the log as events, and the drawn diagram in the widget becomes a *projection* of the program — editor and library are two views of one theory, which is exactly the T-one-architecture-n-ticks shape. The cost: our scheme is deliberately small (fresh environment per eval — flagged in boot.scm's own notes, not built for state), and a congruence-closure engine in it is real work at exactly the moment we want speed of thought.

My candidate: **Racket first, port as the olog library earns its keep** — same as any substrate decision here: think in the fast tool, commit to the home tool when the design stabilizes, keep the Racket file as the spec. The starter API I'd write, roughly:

```scheme
(olog paper
  (type event) (type act) (type log) (type fold) (type lexicon)
  (aspect log :has-as-letters -> event)
  (aspect act :is-an -> event)
  (fact (= (append log act) (letters log)))          ; a path equation
  (check paper orphan-free?)                          ; every aspect has typed ends
  (functor F paper-runtime (event -> box) ...)        ; alignment, checked
  (check F preserves-facts?))                         ; functoriality = a program
```

— types, aspects, facts, checks, functors, and every check returns a verdict that can be logged as an act by actor "linter" (the T-nondeterministic-checks ruling finally gets a producer).

Before I start: which fork — Racket-first-then-port, or straight into the hosted scheme? And one design question worth ruling early because it shapes the library: **is an olog data or type?** I'd say an olog is a *theory* — so `olog.scm` and the ologs it constructs live in git (floor layer, timeless), while only *instances* (functors to Set, i.e., actual events/data) live in the log. That's your floor-is-the-type-layer ruling applied to the new medium — but it means design-by-program happens in git-time, and the log only ever sees the results. Happy medium if you want designing itself to be differentiable: each check-run logs a verdict act, so the *conversation* is in the log even though the *theory* isn't.

Fair — I've been using "git" as shorthand for a role, let me make it concrete.

The project has three kinds of time, and each has its own history medium:

| layer | what lives there | its history |
|---|---|---|
| types (the floor) | lexicons, source code, the olog library itself | **git** |
| instances (the runtime) | events, acts, nodes, geometry | **the log** (`events.jsonl`) |
| the eye | pan/zoom, selection, path | none — ephemeral |

Git plays exactly one role in this: it's the **history medium for the timeless layer**. Right now that's mundane — it versions our code and the `schema/*.json` lexicons, like any repo. The "floor is the type layer" ruling says lexicons change by *editing a file and committing*, never by appending an event — so git is to types what `events.jsonl` is to instances: the place you go to answer "what did this used to be, and who changed it."

Why the split exists at all: the log's letters are *validated by* the types — an act gets checked against a lexicon before it appends. Types can't validate themselves (that's a regress), so they have to live outside the loop, in some medium with versioning of its own. Git is just the pre-built medium we picked for that. The runtime never *queries* git — the server hot-reloads `schema/` from disk, but it doesn't care about commits. Git is for humans asking "when did this type change"; the log is for humans and programs asking "what happened."

So in the lisp-library plan, "git" wasn't a mechanism, just the answer to a placement question: **is an olog a theory or an instance?** If it's a theory (my candidate), then `olog.scm` and the ologs you write with it are *files* — you design by editing and committing, and design history is commit history. Only the *outcomes* — check verdicts, functors applied to real data — would be acts in the log. If you'd rather ologs themselves be runtime objects (drawn, superseded, threaded like nodes are), then git has no role there at all and the whole thing lives in the log — but then ologs become their own instances with no type above them, and the floor thins out.

That's the actual decision hiding under my jargon: does design-by-program happen in file-land or in log-land? File-land (git) buys cheap versioning and no schema needed for the schema; log-land buys differentiability — every design move queryable like everything else. My candidate was file-land for the theory, log-land for verdicts — but it's exactly the kind of call you should make with the tradeoff visible rather than inheriting from me.

Right — an olog is a theory, the way a lexicon is: it says what *kinds* of things can exist and what's true of them, so it lives with the other theories in file-land. Then the log is nothing but Set-valued functors on it — data that the theory makes legible. And "design-by-program" gets a crisp meaning: writing the theory, in a language where the theory checks itself.

That leaves the one open call from before — Racket workbench first, or straight into the hosted scheme. Say the word and I'll start the library.

title: thesis · the medium is a language — shared representation, mediated by projections
body: Named by Julian: the problem the entire project solves is working on a shared underlying representation mediated by PROJECTIONS (UI, markdown, chat, canvas, dot — none is the artifact of record). The representation must be (1) editable by both human and agent, (2) evaluable, (3) deterministic in its effects. Those constraints converge on a Lisp. So: the hosted scheme becomes the canonical representation (not a demo feature); events.jsonl is its evaluation history; the git floor is its type layer (spec outside time, runs inside time); every surface is a fold/projection and never writes back as the primary artifact. Corollary discipline, same spirit as vanilla-forever: the language stays SMALL — every addition is a new thing both parties must hold identically. Pre-echo already in the record: the 9/20 0355 handoff ruled the vault becomes a projection, not the author; boot.scm was a program whose output is a projection; racket/ made the admission formal. Thread E (is the olog the medium) resolves to: the language is the medium; ologs are theories written in it.

text:
The immediate implication, when you're ready for it: the port ruling already tells us where the canonical representation lives — the hosted scheme — and the port happens when `olog.rkt` earns its keep. The design order I'd propose: keep designing theories in Racket (fast, no substrate concerns), let the checks we actually use accumulate into the library's stable core, and port that core — not the ambition — into the runtime's lisp, where verdicts become acts and the projections we already built (including the plane) render the same representation.

But that's the machine's next move, not tonight's. The thing worth sitting with is that the project now has a one-sentence thesis, it's committed, and every piece we've built — log, folds, lexicons, frames, probes, the Racket library — is either already an instance of it or a projection of it. Nothing needs to be thrown away, which is the quiet test of a real thesis.

The center of gravity, as precisely as I can state it: **you are building the external half of a mind, and every experiment is a leak-hunt against re-derivation.**

The one enemy that appears in every corpus, wearing different costumes, is *having to think the same thought again*. Compaction loss. Handoff drift. Cold sessions. Learning decay (the entire Matushak critique sessions). Delegation failures (the agent redoes what it could have used). Provenance doubt (a citation you can't trust forces re-verification). Every system in the vault is a gasket against one of those leaks, and the philosophizing is the search for the gasket material that doesn't itself rot.

Your own corpus sorts into four facets of that one question, and the evidence is specific:

**Memory — what persists.** The vault grammar ruling: journal = events, topic folders = state, undated by design "because a date on a living document is a lie." That is event-sourcing — you discovered it as a *convention* before we built it as a *mechanism*. The filename grammar makes every note findable by construction; threads.yaml is an intent graph so obligations survive sessions; and the 9/20 ruling — "no more handoffs, rehydration = fold/query over the log, the vault becomes a projection" — is the moment the convention admitted it wanted to be a machine. The compaction-tree work is the same hunt at a different scale: END(i)≈START(i+1), chains that lose nothing.

**Form — what the durable representation looks like.** This is what the math shelf *is for*, and it's not math for its own sake: Lawvere's functorial semantics, topos theory, Spivak's ologs, the monoids-and-folds ruling. You keep reaching for formalisms where meaning is compositional and checking is mechanical — because a representation that can't check itself can't be shared with a machine without trusting the machine. The ct-launchpad is you building your own on-ramp to exactly that grammar.

**Protocol — the contract between the halves.** The Builder role assembled from recorded failures, "candidates, never rulings" (which he *wants* articulated before fixes — the 1116 chat says you test exactly this), the prompt-to-action audit's "silence defaults to stop," adjudication debt as the builder's cost, "terminate at relief, not elegance." All of it answers: how does a human and a model think together such that judgment stays yours? And underneath it, the honesty infrastructure — never fabricate provenance, mark the unverified — because a shared mind fails precisely when trust in the record fails.

**Point — why any of it.** `augmentative-content-epistemics.md` names it outright: that's Englebart's program, *Augmenting Human Intellect*. The primers work, the Matuschak critique ("why most learning tools fail"), the whole question of content that makes you more capable versus content that merely occupies you. The success condition of this very partnership is written the same way: more capable *with or without* the partner. Not dependent — compounded.

And here's the thing that makes tonight's thesis feel inevitable rather than new: malleable-paper is the four facets fused into one object. Memory = the log. Form = ologs as runnable theories. Protocol = validated acts, actor-tagged, verdicts as events. Point = a medium you can actually think in with the machine. T-thesis — shared representation, projections as surfaces, the medium is a language — is the *convergence* the whole corpus was circling, arrived at by elimination: handoffs eliminated, prose specs eliminated (not runnable), diagrams eliminated (not evaluable), chat eliminated (not the artifact), agent-as-judge eliminated (judgment must stay yours).

The last observation, and it's the one I'd weigh heaviest: all of this is single-principal by design — no company layer, no generic user, nothing built for strangers. It's not a product and was never going to be. It's a *practice* — the systematic construction of the conditions under which one person's thinking compounds. The prototype-over-scaffolding ruling is the discipline that keeps that practice honest: build the thinking, not the scaffolding for thinking. Which is also why tonight mattered — the olog library is the first artifact in the whole corpus that is simultaneously the theory, the practice, and the machine.

He's sharpening past my framing. I'm still treating the Lisp as a component of a system with other surfaces ("projections," webapp, chat). He's saying: no — the working surface itself IS a program. Not "the app has a lisp core with UIs on top." The workspace = a program. The act of working = writing/evaluating/editing a program. Everything else (chat, webapp) is either absent or auxiliary scaffolding to be shed.

So the picture: the kb, the webapp, chat — these are crutches. The end state: the shared medium between him and me is a program in a lisp — a file/buffer that both of us edit and evaluate. Not "an app that contains a REPL." The session is the program. Thinking = authoring/evaluating the program. The webapp was scaffolding toward the insight; chat is the fallback surface, not the surface.

Like: Smalltalk image? Emacs? Notebook-as-program? But he's saying: stop short of building interfaces; the buffer with the program IS the interface. My responses so far kept slotting Lisp into the app ("hosted scheme becomes canonical, webapp is a projection surface"). He says: invert. There is no app. The webapp was a proving ground; the answer is: work in the program.

Concretely what does this mean for the project? DrRacket session with paper.rkt IS the workspace. My role: co-author of the program — I edit the same file, he edits, we evaluate, verdicts print. Chat remains as fallback for coordination, but the artifact IS the .rkt file. No projection needed because the program is both the representation and the execution — deterministic effects.

Maybe also: effects inside a program need discipline (the act-queue idea maps to: side effects are only performed through designated effect forms; the program's evaluation is otherwise pure). But he said don't keep talking implementation. Acknowledge the inversion precisely, admit the difference from what I said, and state what follows — briefly. What follows: (a) the webapp/chats are scaffolding (the prototype-over-scaffolding ruling now applies to the webapp itself!); (b) the workspace is a program buffer, likely DrRacket + me editing files; (c) what malleable-paper's codebase becomes: not abandoned but demoted — the pieces that matter migrate into the lisp (the log becomes... the program's history? or evaluation trace?); the runtime's role shrinks to: the effect substrate — the only things a program can't do alone are IO/effects and persistence, so the runtime becomes the effects host, not the workspace.

Actually that last point is the one concrete architecture sentence worth saying: programs are pure workspace; effects need a host; so the server survives as the effects host — intake/validation/append — which is already what it is. The UI doesn't survive as the workspace; it survives at most as another effects sink (a display the program can produce, e.g. rendering an olog to a web page is a program effect — the widget becomes a LIBRARY callable from the program, not the canvas you draw in).

Keep it tight. Acknowledge miss, state the inversion, state the one architectural consequence, and maybe end with the concrete next move: our next work session happens in paper.rkt (or a work file), and I edit the program too. Maybe propose: make a workspace file convention — e.g., work.rkt or a journal of programs? Don't over-build. He'll say what's next.

Length: short-medium. This is a "sit with it" moment — don't sprawl.Yes — I hear the correction now. I kept slotting the Lisp *inside* the system I already had: a kernel under a webapp, one projection among many, chat as the conversation layer. You're saying invert it entirely. There is no app with a language in it. **The workspace is a program. Working is authoring and evaluating it.** Chat is the fallback channel, not the surface. The webapp was scaffolding — and by your own ruling (prototype over scaffolding), scaffolding gets shed once it's taught you what it has to teach.

And that actually *closes* the loop on what malleable-paper was for: the drag, the fold, the supersede gestures — that whole interface was us discovering, by use, what the constraints on the shared representation are. Once named, the interface's job is done. It doesn't get ported; it gets *quoted* — the shapes it proved out (types, letters, folds, verdicts) become the vocabulary of the language, and the webapp's remains shrink to an effects host: a program is a pure workspace, but effects (persistence, validation, display) need somewhere to happen. The server already *is* that — validated intake, append, serve. The widget survives, if at all, as a library a program can call to produce a display — not as the canvas.

The honest test of this inversion is behavioral, and it's immediate: our next working session isn't "tell me in chat and I'll change the app." It's you and me editing the same `.rkt` file — the program is the design document, the theory, the tool, and the record of what was tried. DrRacket is enough. That's already true of `paper.rkt`; the difference you're marking is that it's not the prototype *of* the workspace. It *is* the workspace.

What that means for me concretely, as the other party: my unit of contribution stops being "a feature" or "an answer" and becomes edits and expressions in the shared program — small enough for you to read, evaluate, and rule on. Adjudication doesn't change; its *object* changes, from UI behavior to program text.

One thing I'd hold onto from the road here, so the old work isn't lost in the inversion: the gesture vocabulary we validated in the widget (supersede-not-delete, evidence-on-a-mark, reading-as-check) is now **specification, not implementation** — when the program needs those ideas, it gets them as forms, not widgets.
